why: A git status shows touched files in one command, so the raw facts are cheap; what is missing is a declared scope to compare against, and that scope does not exist anywhere for the tool to read either. Any scope-drift verdict is inference, so it will be noisy, and a noisy drift flag gets ignored rather than acted on.

Answering a prompt today is cmd+N or tmux prefix+n away for a shell-competent user: mildly annoying, not unreachable. And the trip does not really disappear, because anything beyond a yes/no still requires reading the surrounding context in the pane; only rubber-stamp approvals actually get faster.

Quota is already one command away in Claude Code and on the status line for anyone running Barista, and Codex prints a usage line natively; the only added work is rolling several harnesses into one verdict. Commodity in waiting too. It would occasionally stop a doomed long job, but in practice people start the job anyway and deal with the wall when it arrives.

Nine harnesses with no cross-session view means finding a blocked pane requires cycling every tab or scripting capture-pane, which nobody does reliably; this is genuine correlation work. A silently blocked session is pure dead time, and clearing it changes behaviour every single day. Vendors may ship per-harness notifications, but all eight of them within a year is not credible.

No harness estimates turn duration at all, so a consolidated next-needed clock is effectively unobtainable by hand. But the impact claim leans on ETAs being trustworthy, and agent turn lengths are famously unpredictable; a wrong 3:40 sends the user back to poll anyway, so the behaviour change is a coffee break rather than a real decision.

The user launched the sessions so partly knows this already, and ps or a look at the working dirs gets close, but at 3 to 12 sessions across worktrees the correlation is exactly what people lose track of. When it fires it prevents concrete loss (clobbered edits, conflicts), which is why impact holds up, though a worktree-disciplined user hits it rarely.

No harness keeps queryable history, so the retrospective genuinely cannot be assembled by hand. But this is the archetypal item that names a real frustration and then assumes a report fixes it: making the case for delegating is a one-off realisation, not a recurring decision, and attention-allocation dashboards get admired once and never opened again.

Knowing which finished sessions you never read requires remembering across time and panes, which is real correlation work. But be honest about the payoff: the pane is usually still sitting there, and much unread output was abandoned on purpose rather than forgotten, so the recovered value is smaller than collect work you already paid for implies.

Stake is not recorded anywhere, but it is not missing either: the user chose what to launch and already carries the consequence in their head, so a machine-inferred stake label is redundant at best. And an inferred consequence ranking is the kind of guess users will not sort their day by once it is wrong twice.

This is already shipped: /usage reports it on demand and Barista caches the 5-hour percentage and reset time straight onto the status line, so many users see it unprompted. Pure commodity. The underlying need is genuine (a mid-task force-pause costs real time and knowing the reset changes what you start), but Cargento adds almost nothing here.
